title: Sectoral Aspects of Indian Economy
summary: ## Three sectors

We use food items (cereals, pulses, fruit, oil) produced by farmers in villages, and non-food items (clothes, shoes, furniture, vehicles) produced by industries in towns and cities. The occupations people follow are grouped into three sectors.
## Primary sector

The primary sector covers (1) agriculture and allied activities such as livestock, poultry and dairy, (2) fishery, (3) forestry — timber, firewood and herbal medicines — and (4) mining and quarrying. These are the traditional rural occupations, and crops give both food and non-food items such as cotton and jute.

Towns and cities are urban areas, such as Jaipur, Pune and Bhubaneswar. Delhi, Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata are metros. Urban areas are known for non-agricultural activities in the secondary and tertiary sectors.
## Secondary sector
The secondary sector covers three activities.
(1) Manufacturing makes goods from raw materials in factories. Small-scale examples are shoes, textiles, printing, glass and furniture; large-scale examples are steel, automobiles and aluminium.
(2) Construction builds houses, roads, bridges, dams and airports. It is a regular activity in both rural and urban areas.
(3) Gas, water and electricity supply.
## Tertiary (service) sector

The service sector includes trade, hotels and restaurants; transport, storage and communication; finance (banking and insurance); real estate and business services; public administration; and other services.
In 2009–10, about 50% of workers were in agriculture, 13.3% in manufacturing and 13.2% in trade and hotels.
## Role of the primary sector (agriculture)
(1) Share in national income: more than 50% at independence, about 15% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: it is the largest employer. About 70% of people depended on it at independence and about 50% in 2009–10.
(3) Food for millions: food-grain output was about 234 million tonnes in 2008–09.
(4) Raw materials for industry: sugar, jute, cotton textiles, vanaspati, paper (from grass and bamboo) and food processing (pickles, jam, juice, biscuits).
## Role of the secondary sector

A small-scale industry needs at least ₹25 lakh of spending on plant and machinery and is mostly labour-intensive. Large-scale industry needs huge capital investment and is capital-intensive, e.g. Tata Steel at Jamshedpur.
(1) Share in national income: 14% at independence, 28% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: about 3.3 crore people work in industry, about 3.12 crore of them in small industries.
(3) Infrastructure: roads, railways, dams (Hirakud, Bhakra-Nangal), buildings and communication towers.
(4) Consumer goods such as clothes, pens, soap, cycles and cars.
Small industries help nation-building, and self-employed people run their own small businesses.
## Role of the service sector
(1) National income: the largest share, 55.2% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: 29.4% of workers. It pays more than agriculture and offers year-round, non-seasonal work, so educated people move to it.
(3) Foreign funds: banking, insurance, trade, transport, hotels and computer services attract foreign direct investment, which creates jobs.
(4) Exports: IT, consultancy and legal services earned about ₹4.35 lakh crore in 2009–10.
## Linkages among the sectors

The sectors support each other. Industry supplies farmers with pumps, fertiliser and tractors, and agriculture supplies food and raw materials to industry. Services — transport (trucks), communication (mobile phones), banking (cheques) and trade (shops) — make these exchanges possible. The farmer Hari Singh sells wheat, buys a diesel pump through a hardware shop, and the same truck carries food back to the industrial town.

sa: Explain the role of the tertiary sector in the Indian economy.

(1) It contributes the largest share of national income — 55.2% in 2009–10.
(2) It employs 29.4% of workers and pays more than agriculture.
(3) It attracts foreign direct investment in banking, insurance, trade, hotels and IT.
(4) It earns foreign exchange through service exports such as IT and consultancy.
Explain the importance of the primary sector.

(1) It produces food for millions — about 234 million tonnes of food grains.
(2) It is the largest employer (about 50% of workers).
(3) It provides raw materials to the sugar, jute, cotton textile, paper and food-processing industries.
(4) It still contributes a share of national income (about 15%).
'The primary sector provides raw materials to industries.' Explain.

Many industries depend on agriculture.
Sugar mills need sugarcane, jute mills need jute, textile mills need cotton, and vanaspati needs oilseeds.
Paper needs grass and bamboo.
The food-processing industry (pickles, jam, juice, biscuits) runs on farm produce.
How are agriculture, industry and services linked?

Industry supplies agriculture with pumps, fertiliser, pesticides and tractors.
Agriculture supplies food and raw materials to industry.
Services — transport, communication, banking and trade — carry goods and money between them. A farmer buys a pump through a shop, pays by money that reaches the factory through a bank, and the truck carries food back to the town.
la: Explain the production activities of the secondary sector and its role in the economy.

Activities: (1) manufacturing — small-scale (shoes, textiles, furniture) and large-scale (steel, automobiles); (2) construction — buildings, roads, bridges, dams; (3) gas, water and electricity supply.
Role: (1) its share of national income rose from 14% at independence to 28% in 2009–10; (2) it employs about 3.3 crore people; (3) it builds infrastructure — roads, railways, dams such as Hirakud and Bhakra-Nangal, towers; (4) it supplies consumer goods such as clothes, soap, cycles and cars.
Explain the importance of the service sector in providing employment and promoting exports.

Employment: the service sector employed 29.4% of workers in 2009–10, and this share is rising. Educated people (graduates, engineers, doctors, professionals) find jobs in banking, IT, transport, education and health. It pays more than agriculture and offers year-round, non-seasonal work.
Exports: India's business services — IT, consultancy and legal services — are of world standard and earned about ₹4.35 lakh crore of foreign exchange in 2009–10. The sector also attracts foreign direct investment, which creates still more jobs.
Explain the role of agriculture in the Indian economy.

(1) National income: more than 50% at independence, about 15% in 2009–10.
(2) Employment: the mainstay of the economy. About 70% of people depended on it at independence and about 50% in 2009–10.
(3) Food: it feeds a large and growing population (234 million tonnes of food grains).
(4) Raw materials: it supplies the sugar, jute, cotton, vanaspati, paper and food-processing industries.
(5) Market: farmers buy industrial goods such as pumps, fertiliser and tractors.
